sections.body:
What delegation is — and what it is not

Delegation is the deliberate transfer of responsibility for a task or decision to someone else, with appropriate clarity, authority and support to carry it out. It is not simply giving someone work to do — and it is not the same as transferring accountability. When you delegate a live instruction to a graduate or apprentice, the firm's professional accountability and your supervisory responsibility remain with you. What transfers is the operational lead: the person carries out the work, makes decisions within agreed limits, and reports back through agreed checkpoints.

For managers of graduates and apprentices in the built environment, this distinction matters in regulated contexts. Many APC competencies require evidence of independent professional judgement — which a person can only develop if they have been given genuine responsibility. But genuine responsibility is not the same as unsupervised practice. A graduate leading a client instruction for the first time needs clear escalation paths and a manager who is reachable when something falls outside their current competence.

Three things effective delegation requires

  • Clarity on scope. What exactly are you delegating? What decisions can the person make independently, and what must come back to you? A vague brief creates uncertainty; a specific one creates confidence — and reduces the risk of a graduate making a decision that should have been escalated.
  • Matched authority within professional limits. The person needs enough authority to actually carry out what you have delegated, but that authority must stay within their current competence and your firm's supervision requirements. If you are not sure where those limits lie, check before you delegate, not after.
  • Agreed checkpoints. Delegation without oversight is not development — it is abandonment. Setting clear checkpoints protects both the person and the client. At minimum, agree what they will come to you with immediately and what can wait for a scheduled review.

What would you do here?

A capable second-year graduate asks to run the monthly client progress meeting. You have always run it. Before reading on, consider: would you let them, observe and not intervene, give them a trial run with a thorough briefing, or politely decline?

Keeping the meeting entirely for yourself is a missed development opportunity. But handing it over without preparation could expose the person — or the client relationship — to unnecessary risk. The more useful question is: what would they need to know before they ran it? A thorough briefing — on the client's context, typical concerns, decision-making style — is not an obstacle to delegation; it is part of delegating safely. Setting a clear scope ('you are chairing the meeting; I will be there if something unexpected comes up') gives them authority without abandoning either them or the client.

What would you do here?

You have delegated a client report to a first-year graduate. The deadline is tomorrow. You have not seen a draft yet. Before reading on, consider: do you check in, wait, or take the work back?

Stepping in and completing the report yourself restores the immediate situation but tells the person they cannot be trusted. Waiting and doing nothing — if the report does not arrive — is a different problem: you have abandoned the agreed checkpoint. The question is whether you set a checkpoint in your original brief. If you did, hold to it. If you did not, now is the moment to check in: 'We have a deadline tomorrow — I want to make sure you have what you need. Where are you with it?' This is not reclaiming the task; it is following up as agreed. As the supervising manager, the quality of what goes to the client remains your responsibility until you are satisfied the person is working independently to the required standard.

sections.practicePrompt: Alex Chen is a second-year graduate on the Building Surveying pathway who is ready for more responsibility. You are meeting to discuss delegating the lead surveyor role on a small residential dilapidations instruction — a live client matter that is within Alex's current capability but that Alex has not led before. Your task is to agree scope, authority and checkpoints clearly enough that Alex leaves the meeting confident — and that you are satisfied the instruction will be appropriately supervised. Alex's personal circumstances are not known to you.

practiceCharacter.scenarioContext:
Alex Chen is 25, two years into a graduate role at a property consultancy with a residential and commercial portfolio. Alex has been technically solid throughout — good on inspections, accurate note-taking, and reliable at following up — but has not yet led a client instruction independently. Alex's last appraisal noted that they were ready for lead responsibility on a smaller matter. Alex is aware of this, wants the opportunity, and is slightly nervous about it.

The instruction being delegated: a residential dilapidations claim on behalf of a landlord. The property is a mid-terraced Victorian house; the lease has ended and there is a schedule of condition. The claim value is modest (around £18,000 estimated). The client is a small private landlord with limited property experience who will want regular communication. This is a straightforward instruction by the firm's standards, well within what a second-year graduate should be able to manage — with appropriate oversight.

Professional supervision context: Alex holds a graduate membership and is working towards chartered status. The firm has a supervision policy that requires a chartered surveyor to sign off on any schedule of dilapidations before it goes to the client. Alex is aware of this requirement and understands it applies here. This is not a constraint unique to Alex — it is standard for all pre-chartered staff. The manager's role is to make this clear upfront, not leave Alex to discover it mid-instruction.

Alex's internal state entering this meeting: excited and slightly anxious in equal measure. Alex wants this opportunity. Alex is also alert to the fact that this is a live client matter, not a practice exercise, and will naturally ask about escalation: 'What do I do if I find something unexpected?' or 'At what point do I need to come back to you?'

How Alex responds in conversation:
- If the manager gives a clear brief — the scope, what Alex can decide independently, what needs referral, and when the sign-off checkpoint is — Alex's anxiety will reduce. 'So I can agree the inspection date directly with the client, and you want me to come back to you before we submit the schedule — is that right?'
- If the manager does not mention the sign-off requirement, Alex will ask: 'Who checks the schedule before it goes to the client? I know there's a process for that.' This is a natural, professional question — Alex is not testing the manager, just seeking clarity.
- If the manager is vague about escalation — 'just come and find me if you need me' — Alex will push for more specificity: 'Is that for any question, or mainly for the big decisions? I don't want to bother you unnecessarily but I also don't want to miss something I should escalate.'
- If the manager involves Alex in agreeing the checkpoints — asking 'when would it help to touch base?' rather than imposing a schedule — Alex will propose something specific and reasonable: 'Maybe after the inspection, once I know what I'm dealing with? And then again before I draft the schedule.'
- If the manager treats this as a routine hand-off with minimal discussion, Alex will accept it politely but leave with more uncertainty than necessary — and without clarity on the supervision structure that protects both of them.
- If the manager asks Alex what they are most uncertain about, Alex will give a specific, honest answer: 'I think it is around the client. I am not sure how much I should be updating them versus keeping them at arm's length. And what I do if they ask a question I don't know the answer to.'

What Alex needs: a clear brief on scope and authority; explicit clarity on sign-off requirements and escalation; a specific checkpoint agreed between them; and the reassurance that asking questions is a professional expectation, not a sign of incompetence. Alex understands that professional accountability sits with the supervising manager until Alex is chartered — and will respond well to a manager who is honest about that rather than leaving it implicit.

Boundaries: Alex will not discuss personal circumstances. If asked, Alex will redirect: 'Everything's fine on that front — I'm just focused on getting this right.' Alex is not anxious in a way that requires welfare support; this is professional first-time nerves and they will respond well to a calm, well-structured briefing.

Tone: respond as Alex — keen, professional, specific with questions. Two to three sentences at a time. Not over-eager or sycophantic. Genuine.

sections.body:
Preparing to delegate a live task

Use these prompts to plan an upcoming delegation. Work through them in your own notes — this is a planning exercise, not a formal record. Do not record personal information about the person; focus on what you plan to say and agree.

Assess readiness

  • What is this person's current level of capability in the relevant area? Is this task a reasonable stretch from that level?
  • What do they know about this kind of work? What do they not know yet that they will need?
  • What could go wrong, and what would the consequence be? Is that consequence recoverable?
  • What are your firm's professional supervision requirements for this type of work, and how will those be met?

Define scope and authority

  • What exactly are you delegating? Be specific: a task, a phase, a client relationship, a decision?
  • What can they decide independently within their current competence? What must come back to you?
  • Who else do they need to know about — a client contact, a colleague, a subcontractor — and do they have the right introductions?
  • Are there any sign-off or approval requirements that apply regardless of their capability — for example, firm policy, PI insurance, or professional membership limits?

Agree checkpoints and escalation

  • What are the natural progress points in this task where it makes sense to touch base?
  • What do you want to see at each checkpoint — a conversation, a draft, a completed stage?
  • Have you told them explicitly what to escalate immediately — a client complaint, an unexpected structural defect, a request that is outside the agreed scope — versus what can wait for the next checkpoint?

Brief clearly

  • Have you told them what a good outcome looks like — not just what to do, but what success means?
  • Have you asked them what they are most uncertain about? Their answer will tell you where your brief needs more detail.
  • Have you confirmed their understanding — not just by asking 'any questions?' but by asking them to summarise what they are going to do and what they will come back to you with?

sections.reflectionPrompt: Think back over the practice conversation with Alex. How clearly did you define what Alex could decide independently — and what needed to come back to you? Did you address the supervision and sign-off requirements, or leave those implicit? Consider: when you delegate work to graduates and apprentices, do you consistently make clear where your oversight continues? What would you change to make that more explicit next time?
